facts.statement: Wingegyps lived during the Late Pleistocene, specifically within the Ensenadan and Lujanian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Pleistocene (Ensenadan-Lujanian)~

facts.statement: The first remains assigned to Wingegyps were discovered by Danish scientist Peter Wilhelm Lund in Brazil.
facts.quote: The first remains now assigned to Wingegyps were discovered by Danish scientist Peter Wilhelm Lund after his move to Brazil.

facts.statement: The species name 'cartellei' honors Brazilian paleontologist Castor Cartelle for excavating the site of the holotype.
facts.quote: The species name honors Brazilian paleontologist Castor Cartelle, who excavated fossil material at the site where the holotype was discovered.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Wingegyps fed on fruit or scavenged scraps to avoid competition with larger vultures, as its precise ecology remains unclear.
facts.quote: The precise ecology of Wingegyps is unclear, but it has been suggested that it could have potentially fed on fruit or scraps from carcasses to avoid competition with larger, more powerful vultures.

facts.statement: Stucchi and Emslie describe Wingegyps as being no larger than a raven.
facts.quote: Stucchi and Emslie more broadly describe Wingegyps as "no larger than a raven".

facts.statement: The most prominent feature of Wingegyps is its extremely small size compared to other vultures and condors.
facts.quote: The feature most prominently highlighted regarding Wingegyps is its diminutive size.

facts.statement: In Wingegyps, the foramen magnum opens entirely posteriorly and the occipital condyle is fully visible from the side, unlike in other condors where it is often obscured.
facts.quote: The foramen magnum opens entirely posteriorly rather than showing some degree of ventral deflection and the occipital condyle is visible in its entirety alongside its stalk when looking at the skull from the side, while in other condors it is either obscured entirely (as in Breagyps) or at least partially covered (as is the case in modern condors).

facts.statement: The morphology of the Wingegyps cranium suggests affinities with the major branch of vultures that includes the Andean and Californian condors.
facts.quote: However, the morphology of the Bahia cranium instead suggests affinities with the other major extant branch which includes the Andean and Californian condor as well as several fossil forms.

facts.statement: Degrange and colleagues consider king vultures to be an intermediate form between vultures and condors, but not true condors.
facts.quote: Degrange and colleagues meanwhile consider king vultures to be an intermediate between vultures and condors, but not a true condor.

facts.statement: Fossils of Wingegyps have been found in the states of Minas Gerais and Bahia in Brazil.
facts.quote: Remains of Wingegyps are known from Minas Gerais and Bahia in Brazil

facts.statement: Remains of Wingegyps have also been discovered in Venezuela.
facts.quote: the latter discovery of Wingegyps remains from Venezuela

facts.statement: The genus Wingegyps was described by Alvarenga and Olson in 2004.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Alvarenga & Olson, 2004

facts.statement: The species Wingegyps cartellei was described by Alvarenga and Olson in 2004.
facts.quote: species_authority: Alvarenga & Olson, 2004

facts.statement: The generic name Wingegyps combines the Greek word for vulture with 'Winge' to honor Danish ornithologist Oluf Winge.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico viene de la combinación del vocablo griego gyps, que significa buitre y Winge, en honor al ornitólogo danés Oluf Winge

facts.statement: The specific name cartellei honors paleontologist Cástor Cartelle from the Federal University of Minas Gerais.
facts.quote: En cuanto a su nombre específico, este hace referencia al paleontólogo Cástor Cartelle, de la Universidad Federal de Minas Gerais

facts.statement: The North American Classification Committee of the AOU and the International Ornithological Congress adopted the classification of Wingegyps within the order Accipitriformes.
facts.quote: Esta última posición fue adoptada por la Comisión de Clasificación Norteamericana de la AOU y por el Congreso Ornitológico Internacional

facts.statement: Wingegyps was a small bird, even smaller than the black vulture (Coragyps atratus).
facts.quote: Es de pequeño tamaño, siendo incluso menor que el gallinazo (Coragyps atratus)

facts.statement: Wingegyps differs from other condor genera by having the occipital condyle fully visible from a lateral view.
facts.quote: Se diferencia de otros géneros de cóndores por la total visibilidad desde una vista lateral del cóndilo occipital

facts.statement: If Wingegyps lacked the sense of smell like its close relatives in the genus Cathartes, it would have struggled to compete with them for small carcasses.
facts.quote: Si se supone que al igual que sus parientes cercanos del género Cathartes en cuanto a la carencia de capacidad olfatoria, Wingegyps tendría poco éxito compitiendo con cualquiera de las especies de este género por la obtención de pequeños cadáveres

facts.statement: Wingegyps may have been ecologically equivalent to the palm-nut vulture, feeding on the soft mesocarp of the Paraguay nut (Acrocomia aculeata).
facts.quote: Sin embargo, es probable que sea el equivalente ecológico del buitre palmero (Gypohierax angolensis), en África, alimentándose del suave mesocarpio de la nuez de Paraguay (Acrocomia aculeata)

facts.statement: Alternatively, Wingegyps may have subsisted on scraps left by larger vulture species, similar to the Egyptian vulture.
facts.quote: aunque también podría tener hábitos similares al alimoche común (Neophron percnopterus) subsistiendo con las sobras de otras especies más grandes de buitres

facts.statement: Wingegyps likely lived during the Late Pleistocene or Early Holocene.
facts.quote: Vivió probablemente durante el Pleistoceno superior o el Holoceno inferior

facts.statement: The time range for Wingegyps is estimated from 0.129 to 0.0117 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Late Pleistocene to Late Pleistocene (0.129 to 0.0117 million years ago)

facts.statement: The taxonomic position of the family containing Wingegyps is debated, with authors placing it in Falconiformes, Ciconiiformes, Cathartiformes, or Accipitriformes.
facts.quote: La posición taxonómica de esta familia ha sido objeto de debate de los ornitólogos siendo clasificado dentro de los órdenes de Falconiformes, Ciconiiformes, Cathartiformes y Accipitriformes dependiendo del autor

facts.statement: It is debated whether Wingegyps went extinct because it relied on large carcasses that disappeared alongside American megafauna.
facts.quote: Esta última opción explicaría su extinción ya que al igual que las grandes especies de buitres americanos desapareció casi al mismo tiempo que la megafauna americana

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Olson propose that Wingegyps may have behaved similarly to specialized Old World vultures like the Egyptian vulture or palm-nut vulture.
facts.quote: the team instead proposes that Wingegyps may have acted more similar to some specialized Old World vultures, in particular the Egyptian vulture or palm-nut vulture

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Olson favor the scavenging hypothesis over frugivory because Wingegyps went extinct with South American megafauna while palm trees remain widespread.
facts.quote: Alvarenga and Olson favor the scavenging hypothesis, as Wingegyps seems to have gone extinct at around the same time as South America's megafauna and many other scavengers, whereas palm trees remain widespread until today
